part_0_duplicate_resolution.filename_discrepancy: The task refers to 'pdk_dsent.txt', which does not exist anywhere in this repository (confirmed: grep -rl pdk_dsent . returns nothing). The file matching the exact description given -- two StdCell->AvailableSizes definitions, a 10-entry list then a 7-entry list, with the exact values quoted -- is tech/tech_models/7FinFET.txt (10-entry at line 184, 7-entry at line 205, pre-edit). Proceeding on the assumption this is the intended file. IMPORTANT: none of my own prior DFFRAM sizing work in this project used 7FinFET.txt -- every prior measurement used tech/tech_models/Bulk22LVT.model, which has a SINGLE, non-duplicated StdCell->AvailableSizes definition (10 entries, indices 0-9, at line 198) and was never affected by this bug at all. See the note on Part 5 below.

q1_parser_and_behavior.class: LibUtil::readFile(const char*, std::map<String,String>&) -- libutil/Config.cc:31-117. Called from TechModel::readFile() -- tech/TechModel.cc:58-61 (which itself is called once per tech file/INCLUDE from DSENT's model-construction entry points).
q1_parser_and_behavior.duplicate_key_behavior: LAST-WINS. libutil/Config.cc:115: `config[key] = line;  // overwrites if key is repeated` -- the comment is the code's own, not mine. std::map::operator[] assignment on an existing key overwrites the stored value; the file is read top-to-bottom in one pass, so whichever occurrence appears LATER in the file wins.
q1_parser_and_behavior.consequence_for_7FinFET_txt_pre_edit: The 7-entry list (originally at line 205, AFTER the 10-entry list at line 184) was ALREADY the one in effect for any run using this file, even before this task's edit -- last-wins means the second definition silently overrides the first regardless of which one a reader's eye lands on first.

q2_which_list_was_in_effect_for_index_9_.answer: Neither list in 7FinFET.txt produced the index-9 results referenced. Index 9 requires a 10-element list (indices 0-9); 7FinFET.txt's EFFECTIVE list (last-wins, see above) has only 7 elements (indices 0-6), so index 9 is structurally impossible to obtain from this file regardless of which definition 'wins'. Every 'stage index 9' result in this project's prior reports (e.g. enable_stage_idx:[0,0,0,4,9] at (512,256) in docs/enable_buf_taper_fix_findings.json) came from tech/tech_models/Bulk22LVT.model, whose own StdCell->AvailableSizes (tech/tech_models/Bulk22LVT.model:198) is a SINGLE, non-duplicated 10-entry list -- index 9 there is the legitimate, unambiguous top of that list, uncontaminated by any duplicate-key issue. The duplication in 7FinFET.txt is real and worth fixing, but it is not the explanation for any previously-reported index-9 result.

q3_warning_on_duplicate.answer: No. Read the complete libutil/Config.cc:readFile() function (31-117): the only ASSERT calls are for a failed file open (line 34) and a line with no '=' delimiter (line 73). There is no check, log line, or warning of any kind for a key being seen more than once -- the second occurrence silently replaces the first with no trace.

enable.note: single stage, no ratio to compute
THREE consecutive minimum-size stages (indices 0,1,2 all at size 1.0) before any increase -- two of the three transitions between them are ratio=1.0 padding

mechanism.source_location: model/electrical/DFFRAM.cc: computeChainStages() (anonymous namespace, ~line 101-113) picks stage COUNT as ceil(log(count)/log(taper)), a formula that assumes a CONTINUOUS size range achievable at every step. sizeBufChain() (~line 51-71) then sizes each stage working backward from the real load, dividing the target by `taper` each step (line ~62: `target /= fanout_;` -- the parameter is literally named fanout_ inside this now-shared helper, a naming leftover from before the EnableFanout/EnableTaper split; it receives whatever taper value the caller passes) and picking the LARGEST available discrete size <= that target.
mechanism.plain_language: Stage COUNT is decided first, purely from N/B and the taper ratio, with NO knowledge of what sizes are actually available in the tech file. Sizing happens SECOND, and once the shrinking target falls below the SMALLEST available size (1.0 in the 7-entry FinFET list), every remaining stage working back toward the source has nothing smaller to pick -- they all clamp to the minimum. With only 7 discrete sizes spanning a 1x-16x range, and a stage count formula computed as if sizes were continuous, it is common for the formula to demand more stages than the discrete size range can actually support distinct sizes for -- the excess stages toward the source become pure padding: added series delay (each stage still has its own nonzero intrinsic gate delay) with literally zero sizing benefit (ratio exactly 1.0, identical Ron).
mechanism.not_fixed: Per instructions, mechanism reported only -- computeChainStages()/sizeBufChain() not modified in this task.

part_3_data.physical_explanation_of_taper_direction: At stages=1, a LARGER taper shrinks the single stage's sizing target MORE (target=final_load/taper), which can UNDER-size the stage below what the real load needs (bad when the load is genuinely large -- N=64,512 cases: smaller taper, i.e. LESS division, correctly lets the target stay high enough to reach the max available size). But for a genuinely SMALL load (small N), the largest available driver is actually WORSE than a right-sized one (an oversized buffer's own intrinsic self-capacitance dominates when the load it drives is tiny) -- so a LARGER taper, which deliberately under-targets and picks a smaller, better-matched size, wins there. This is why (4,32) prefers taper~1.4-2 (moderate) while the three larger points are indifferent to taper once it's below ~1.5 (already saturated at the max available size regardless).
part_3_data.not_a_default_change: Findings reported only; no default was changed.

part_4_depth_scaling.methodology: Full (stages in {1..6}) x (taper in {1.0,1.2,1.4,1.5,2,2.5,3,4,6}) search independently AT EACH of the 8 standard N values (4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512), B=32 fixed, RowClock held at default -- this is the Part-3-style interior-optimum search repeated per N, not a reuse of only the 4 canonical points.

settings_vary_non_monotonically_with_N.stages: CONSTANT at 1 for every single N -- monotonic (trivially) in the coarsest sense.
settings_vary_non_monotonically_with_N.taper: NON-MONOTONIC: 2 -> 4 -> 6 -> 6 -> 1.0 -> 1.0 -> 1.0 -> 1.0. Rises through N=4..32, then DROPS SHARPLY and stays flat for N=64..512.
settings_vary_non_monotonically_with_N.regime_boundary: The drop happens between N=32 and N=64 -- exactly where enable_load grows large enough that even taper=1.0 (weakest shrink) already saturates the single stage at the max available size (16.0). Below that boundary, the optimal taper is actively selecting a right-sized (non-maximal) driver; above it, sizing is degenerate (any taper<=~1.5 gives the same, max-sized, answer).

part_4_depth_scaling.verdict: This R^2 (0.805) is LOWER than the prior taper-task's 0.894, despite this search being far more exhaustive (every N searched individually over a 6x9 grid, all edges extended and verified, versus the prior task's smaller, less complete search). A grid-search artifact would predict R^2 IMPROVING as the search gets more thorough, since a better search should find delay values closer to whatever smooth curve underlies them. Instead it got WORSE. This is the data supporting genuine circuit non-monotonicity, specifically the discrete regime change identified above (load-matching mode below N~64, saturation mode above it) -- a real qualitative kink in the delay-vs-N relationship that no single log-linear model can fit well, independent of how carefully each point's own optimum is searched. The data does NOT support 'the R^2 drop was a grid-search artifact' -- a more careful search made it worse, not better.
